## What it is

A self-cleaning oven doesn't need outside help to stay working. Gelman's point is that statistical software should work the same way. A package that fits a model should include a way to *check that it fits the model correctly*, typically by simulating fake data from known parameter values, fitting the model, and confirming that the parameters are recovered.

## Why it matters

Statistical code fails silently. A wrong standard-error formula, an indexing bug or a mis-specified prior still produces numbers that look plausible. Without a built-in self-test, these errors spread into published results. Fake-data simulation is the cheapest and most general check available, because it compares the code against a case where you *know* the right answer.

## How it works

1. Choose true parameter values $\theta^*$.
2. Simulate data $y^{\text{fake}} \sim p(y \mid \theta^*)$ using the *same* model the code claims to fit.
3. Run the fitting code on $y^{\text{fake}}$ and record the estimate and interval.
4. Repeat many times. Estimates should centre on $\theta^*$, and 95% intervals should cover $\theta^*$ about 95% of the time.

Simulation-based calibration (SBC) extends this to Bayesian samplers by drawing $\theta^*$ from the prior.

## Simulated example

Our "package" estimates a treatment effect from a two-group experiment and reports a 95% interval. One version has a subtle bug: it forgets one group's variance when computing the standard error. Run the built-in fake-data check and see whether the bug is caught.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, mean, variance, fmt, pct} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof buggy = Inputs.toggle({label: "Introduce the standard-error bug", value: true})
viewof nFake = Inputs.range([50, 1000], {value: 300, step: 50, label: "Fake datasets"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 18, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
fakeCheck = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const truth = 0.4, n = 50;
  return range(nFake).map(k => {
    const t = r.normals(n, truth, 1), c = r.normals(n, 0, 1);
    const est = mean(t) - mean(c);
    const se = buggy ? Math.sqrt(variance(t) / n) : Math.sqrt(variance(t) / n + variance(c) / n);
    const lo = est - 1.96 * se, hi = est + 1.96 * se;
    return {k, est, lo, hi, covered: lo <= truth && truth <= hi, truth};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  x: {label: "Fake dataset (first 80 shown)"},
  y: {label: "Estimate with 95% interval", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(fakeCheck.slice(0, 80), {x: "k", y1: "lo", y2: "hi", stroke: d => d.covered ? "#2166ac" : "#d6604d"}),
    Plot.dot(fakeCheck.slice(0, 80), {x: "k", y: "est", r: 2, fill: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.4], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const cov = fakeCheck.filter(d => d.covered).length / fakeCheck.length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Nominal coverage 95%. Observed coverage over ${nFake} fake datasets: **${pct(cov, 1)}**. ${cov < 0.92 ? "The self-test flags a problem: the intervals are too narrow. Without the test, every individual output would have looked perfectly reasonable." : "Coverage is close to nominal, so the code passes its own test."}`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Every model-fitting routine should come with a fake-data check: simulate from known parameters, refit, and confirm recovery.
- Check coverage, not just point estimates. Bugs in uncertainty are the hardest to see.
- Self-testing code makes later changes safe, because you'll know at once if something broke.
:::
